approaches.name: Slack as control plane
approaches.summary: Use Slack (issues channel + bot channels) as the company's control plane before adding Linear/etc. Humans and bots collaborate in threads; bots can be @-mentioned to ship features.
steps: Wire bots to listen (e.g. Ping routines)
Treat Slack as triage + assignment surface
approaches.when_to_use: Day-0 company setup; mixed human+bot orgs
anti_patterns: Jumping to heavy PM tools before Slack is working

approaches.name: Ship to main (no PRs) early-stage policy
approaches.summary: After Steve opened a huge PR, Lauren set rule: no pull requests — ship to main until someone objects. Optimized for 72-hour velocity; later evolves into small-PR autopilot + Play QA + mash.

approaches.name: Poteto mode
approaches.summary: P-Stack router skill: invoke via /poteto mode or natural language. Routes into playbooks (prototyping with debug sliders, architect multi-model review, full autopilot). Described as adding flavor/constraints awareness via multi-model swarm.
steps: Install P-Stack / ensure potato skills present
Optionally specify playbook: prototyping | architect | full autopilot
Let router spawn cloud agents as needed
approaches.when_to_use: Fast prototypes; structured eng loops; overnight factories
anti_patterns: Skipping architect when constraints matter — or over-architecting early (Lauren skipped architect for speed)

approaches.name: Full autopilot
approaches.summary: Poteto-mode playbook that breaks a plan into small phases, implements small PRs, verifies (run app, fuzz/click), then auto-merges when checks pass. Used overnight day2→day3 for 100–170+ PRs.
steps: slash poteto mode → full autopilot this plan
approaches.when_to_use: When you want high PR throughput with verification loops
anti_patterns: Calling it pure YOLO without verification
Using full autopilot on unvalidated triage (day3: Crumble→Tater without full autopilot)

approaches.name: Swarm
approaches.summary: Spin many Cursor Cloud Agents / poteto-mode agents (often different models) in parallel to generate and compare prototypes or critique architecture. Used day2 morning to explore game prototypes.
approaches.when_to_use: Early ideation; architect critique; frontend prototyping forks

approaches.name: Teach a task
approaches.summary: Human drives the bot's computer to demonstrate a UI workflow (e.g. add animation). Recording becomes a reusable skill the bot can replay later without re-teaching.
approaches.when_to_use: Repetitive GUI workflows (Slides, Forms, design tools)

approaches.name: Auto-review
approaches.summary: Baseline classifier decides risky vs safe actions; users add personal rules (e.g. never send email without asking). Credentials via modal on human machine, not bot VM. Memory of permissions builds trust over time.
approaches.when_to_use: Any connector with side effects (email, Slack external, payments)

approaches.name: Long-lived memory (S3)
approaches.summary: Bot memory persists in S3 buckets — long-lived across tasks. Steering ('never use my full name') is stored forever. Duplicate bots get fresh context. Humans must update memory when delegated bots are deleted.
steps: Update CoS when team membership changes
approaches.when_to_use: Persona bots used across many projects
anti_patterns: Assuming deleted sub-bots are known to CoS without update

approaches.summary: Put delegation in the CoS description so it never does specialist work itself — always routes to subordinates with right context. Human mostly talks to Steve; Eggbot/meta-bot maintains the org chart.

approaches.name: Implementer vs reviewer bots
approaches.summary: Separate bots that write code from bots that review/validate (Tater vs Hashbrown; Emily EM who doesn't code). Reduces self-approval bias; Play adds runtime QA beyond static review.
anti_patterns: Same bot merges its own unverified work
